messages.content: How does venture capital actually work?

VC funds raise capital from LPs (pension funds, endowments, family offices), deploy it into ~20-30 startups per fund, and return capital + profit to LPs over a 10-year fund life. VC operates on power law: one investment must return the entire fund (the 'fund returner'). This means VCs only invest in companies that could be worth £100M+ in 7-10 years — not good businesses, but potentially massive ones. Mechanics: pre-seed/seed (£250K-£2M, 15-25% equity, idea or early product), Series A (£2-15M, proven PMF, scaling team), Series B+ (£15M+, scaling revenue). VC is expensive capital — it comes with board seats, pro-rata rights, and liquidation preferences. Only appropriate for businesses targeting massive markets.
What should a startup pitch deck contain?

Problem (1 slide): what pain, for whom, how big? Solution (1-2 slides): your answer — show don't tell. Market size (1 slide): TAM/SAM/SOM — be honest, investors verify. Business model (1 slide): how do you make money? Traction (1 slide): the most important slide — what evidence do you have that this works? Team (1 slide): why are you the right people to solve this? Competition (1 slide): who else is doing this and why are you different? Financials (1 slide): 3-year projections with assumptions shown. Ask (1 slide): how much, at what valuation, what it will fund. Investors invest in people first, market second, product third. The deck gets you the meeting; the team closes the round.
What is product-market fit and how do you know when you have it?

Product-market fit (Marc Andreessen): the product is in a good market and can satisfy that market. Indicators: organic growth (users sharing without incentive), high retention (users return repeatedly), strong Net Promoter Score, and — most clearly — the 40% rule (Sean Ellis): if less than 40% of users would be 'very disappointed' if the product disappeared, you don't have PMF. Before PMF: every growth dollar is wasted because the product is leaking. After PMF: growth compounds. The biggest mistake: scaling marketing before PMF — you accelerate learning that the product doesn't work. Stay in search mode until PMF is clear, then switch to scale mode.
What are the most important metrics for a SaaS startup?

Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR): predictable subscription revenue per month. Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC): total sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired. Customer Lifetime Value (LTV): average revenue per customer ÷ churn rate. LTV:CAC ratio: must be >3:1 for sustainable growth — below this you're paying more to acquire customers than you'll ever recover. Churn rate: percentage of customers lost per month. 2% monthly = 22% annually. In SaaS, churn is the silent killer — even excellent acquisition cannot overcome high churn. Net Revenue Retention (NRR): if existing customers expand their contracts enough, NRR can exceed 100% — growth from existing customers without new acquisition.
